identity.plain_name: Screw holes stretched into slots, so a part such as a motor can be slid along a little and then clamped tight; often a separate screw pushes or pulls it along, so you can tighten a belt or chain and line it up before locking it
identity.term: Slotted adjustment with a jacking screw (slotted mount, sliding motor plate, adjustable centres)
aliases: slotted holes, slotted mounting holes, elongated holes, oblong slots, short-slotted and long-slotted holes (structural steel terms, RCSC)
slotted mount, slotted bracket, sliding motor plate, adjustable motor mount, motor tensioner (3D-printer and robot-kit term)
motor slide rails, slide base, adjustable motor base (industrial; automatic motor bases add a spring)
jacking screw, jack bolt, jackbolt, pusher screw, adjusting screw, tensioning screw, draw bolt
adjustable centres, adjustable centre distance, take-up, centre-distance allowance (belt and chain drive terms, Gates)
chain tug, chain tensioner screw, 'banjo bolt' (BMX), chain adjuster (motorcycles)
horizontal dropout, track fork end, rear-facing forkend (bicycles: the axle slides in a slot)
pivoting motor plate with an arc slot, alternator adjusting bracket (a hinge plus a curved slot)
identity.one_liner: A part is fixed with screws through slots instead of round holes, so it can be slid to set a belt or chain tension or line it up, usually pushed by a separate adjusting (jacking) screw, and is then locked by tightening the screws.
identity.complexity: A few parts: a base, plate or rails with slots (or a part with slotted feet), clamping screws or bolts with washers through the slots, a fixed lug, block or nut with a threaded hole for the jacking screw, the jacking screw itself (often with a lock nut), and sometimes a scale or index marks. The moving part is a motor, an idler pulley, a bearing block or a wheel axle.
identity.how_it_works: The clamping screws pass through slots, so while they are loose the part can slide along the slot but not sideways. A jacking screw, threaded through a fixed lug, pushes or pulls the part along a little for each turn, giving a fine, controlled move and stopping it from springing back while you work. When the belt or chain is tight enough, or the part is lined up, the clamping screws are tightened and friction under their heads locks it; the jacking screw also acts as a backstop against the belt's pull. On Prusa's MK3/MK4 X axis you slightly release the motor screws so 'the motor must be able to move', turn the screw at the back of the X-end to tension the belt, then tighten the motor screws again.

job: tighten and hold tension: sets the tension of a belt or chain by moving a motor, idler or axle, then holds it
line parts up exactly: lines up pulleys, sprockets, shafts or a sensor before clamping
join and hold: once clamped it is an ordinary screwed joint
finder_attributes.motion: slide while adjusting, over the length of the slot (typically a few millimetres to a few centimetres) [uncertain: no typical figure opened]; none once clamped. Pivoting versions rotate a few degrees about a hinge bolt while a bolt slides in an arc slot (Wikimedia Commons alternator tensioner photo)
finder_attributes.degrees_of_freedom: 0 once clamped. While adjusting, 1 (along the slot) if the slots and screws guide it well; with only one screw or wide slots it can also twist, so 2, which is why two jacking screws or a guide edge are used.
special_behaviour: tensioning (takes up slack and holds): moving the motor or axle takes up belt or chain slack, then the clamping screws hold that setting; it is set by hand, not automatic

self-locking (holds under load, won't back-drive): the jacking screw's thread doesn't turn back under the belt's pull, because screw threads are self-locking (Wikipedia 'Jackscrew'), so it holds the setting even while the clamping screws are loose
finder_attributes.holding_principle: friction or clamping (force-fit): the clamping screws squeeze the part onto its base; plus shape (form-fit) where the jacking screw butts against the part or lug and stops it sliding back along the slot. Structural practice notes that a load along a slot is carried only by friction (a slip-critical joint), whereas a load across the slot bears on the bolt (UMD notes on RCSC 2000)
finder_attributes.input_output: An adjuster, not a drive: turning the jacking screw -> a small straight movement of one thread pitch per turn (0.5 mm for M3, 0.7 mm for M4, 0.8 mm for M5 coarse threads, Wikipedia 'ISO metric screw thread'); arrangement in line with the slot. Back-drivable: no, thread friction holds it (Wikipedia 'Jackscrew').
finder_attributes.removability: removable: undo the clamping screws and slide the part out; the setting is lost unless you mark it or leave the jacking screw where it is
finder_attributes.reuse_cycles: effectively unlimited with metal screws in metal threads or nuts; fewer when the jacking screw turns in a printed thread, which wears (use inserts or captive nuts, Hubs)
finder_attributes.tools_needed: hex key or spanner (Prusa uses a 2.5 mm hex key for all its belt adjustments); a straightedge or laser tool to check pulley alignment (IronHorse motor base instructions); optionally a belt-tension gauge or phone app
finder_attributes.load: Light to heavy, depending on the screws: from M3 screws on a printer motor to steel slide rails under large electric motors (US Motors; Soco). Strong across the slot, where the bolts bear on the slot sides; along the slot it holds only by clamping friction unless the jacking screw or a stop backs it up (UMD notes on RCSC 2000: slotted holes are normally placed with the slot across the load). Shock or vibration along the slot can make it creep.
finder_attributes.adjustable: yes: that is its purpose. Loosen the clamping screws, turn the jacking screw (or slide by hand), re-tighten; re-adjust as belts and chains stretch (Tsubaki: chain elongates 0.05 to 0.1 % early in use, so adjustment is required)
finder_attributes.play_and_precision: No play once clamped. Fine resolution with a jacking screw: an M3 screw moves 0.5 mm per turn, so a quarter turn is about 0.12 mm (arithmetic from the thread pitch). The part can twist in its slots while loose and may shift a little as the clamping screws are tightened, so check alignment after locking [uncertain: no figure opened]. Belt drives tolerate only small misalignment (Gates: synchronous belts no more than 1/4 degree or 1/16 in per foot). Not a repeatable locator: use pins or a hole-and-slot pair when the part must return to exactly the same place.
finder_attributes.access_needed: one side only (blind) when the clamping screws go into tapped holes, T-slot nuts or captive nuts; both sides when through-bolts and nuts are used; the jacking screw needs room for a hex key or spanner along its axis
finder_attributes.materials: Steel or aluminium plates and rails (industrial slide rails are fabricated galvanised steel, Soco), printed brackets in PETG, ASA or ABS (Printables 338646 is printed in ABS or ASA), plywood or MDF bases with slots routed or cut; steel screws with washers. Hard materials hold best; soft wood and plastics need large washers because the screw heads sink in and creep.
finder_attributes.maker_difficulty: easy: slots print, laser-cut or rout easily and need only ordinary screws, washers and a nut or insert for the jacking screw

processes: 3D print (FDM): slotted motor brackets and tensioners with captive nuts or heat-set inserts
laser cut: slotted plates in acrylic, plywood or metal
CNC: milled slots in aluminium or steel plates
woodwork: routed or drilled-and-joined slots in a wooden base
sheet metal: slotted brackets and bent lugs for the jacking screw
off-the-shelf part: motor slide rails and bases, adjustable motor mounts, chain tugs
making.print_in_place: partly: a slotted bracket with its jacking-screw lug prints as one piece, but it needs screws, washers and nuts or threaded inserts before it works (Printables 338646 needs two M3x40 screws and two M3 heat-set inserts)
making.making_tips_3d_printing: Print slotted plates lying flat so the slots are formed in the XY plane, where outlines are most accurate and the clamping force runs along the layers rather than prising them apart (QIDI blog on clamping force direction; Prusa on orientation and tolerances) [uncertain: no source tests slots specifically]. Make the slot as wide as a normal clearance hole for the screw and as long as the travel you need plus spare for belt stretch (Gates tensioning allowance). Put a washer under every screw head on a slot; one designer of a slotted NEMA 17 bracket notes it is 'probably a good idea to add washers' (Printables 217277), and washers stop heads sinking into plastic (QIDI blog). Don't let the jacking screw cut its own thread in the print: use a heat-set insert or a captive nut (Printables 338646 uses brass threaded inserts), with at least one screw diameter of plastic round it and a nut pocket about 0.2 mm larger than the nut (Hubs). Give the lug the jacking screw pushes against plenty of perimeters and infill, because it carries the full belt pull. Use PETG, ASA or ABS rather than PLA near warm motors: PLA softens above about 60 °C and creeps under constant load (Prusa PLA page; Thrinter creep test). Re-check tension after a few hours of use, because printed parts and new belts settle.
making.off_the_shelf_parts: Search terms: 'adjustable motor mount', 'slotted motor mount', 'NEMA 17 motor bracket slotted', 'motor slide rails', 'motor slide base', 'adjustable motor base', 'automatic motor base' (spring-loaded), 'belt tensioner screw', 'jack bolt' or 'jacking screw', 'chain tug' or 'chain tensioner' (bicycle), 'track fork ends' or 'horizontal dropouts', 'idler pulley with slotted bracket', 'T-slot nut' (for sliding along aluminium extrusion), 'flat washer', 'heat-set insert', 'nylon-insert lock nut'.
rules_of_thumb: Always leave room to move: Gates says fixed-centre belt drives are not recommended and gives a minimum centre-distance allowance for installing and for tensioning; for a synchronous belt 500 to 1000 mm long it is 1.8 mm shorter to fit the belt (sprockets removed) and 0.8 mm longer to tension it, with extra if the belt must go over flanged sprockets (Gates PowerGrip GT2 Drive Design Manual, Table 4, https://static.chipdip.ru/lib/569/DOC010569405.pdf).

If you must use fixed centres, Gates limits them to lightly loaded or motion-transfer drives and says the centre distance must be held within about 0.05 to 0.08 mm, because belt tension can vary by a factor of 3 or more from tolerance stack-up (same manual, section 11).

Keep pulleys lined up while sliding: synchronous belt misalignment should not exceed 1/4 degree or 1/16 in per foot (Gates, same manual); move the motor with the adjusting screw only to keep its alignment (IronHorse automatic motor base instructions, https://cdn.automationdirect.com/static/manuals/ironhorsemotorbases/ihautobaseinstall.pdf); with two adjusters, turn both an equal number of turns and check the index marks match (Honda CB400 owner's manual p. 60, https://www.bike-parts.fr/thumbs/pdf_url/img/owner_manuals/CB400B/2500_2500/0063.pdf).

Chains: set slack to about 4 % of the span (32 mm on an 800 mm span), or about 2 % for vertical drives, spans over 1 m, heavy frequent starts or reversing; re-adjust as the chain stretches 0.05 to 0.1 % early on (Tsubaki Installation & Maintenance Guide p. 15, https://catalog.ustsubaki.com/view/303394094/15/).

Put slots across the main load where you can; a load along the slot is held only by friction, which is why structural codes treat such joints as slip-critical and use washers over slots (UMD lecture notes summarising RCSC 2000, https://user.eng.umd.edu/~ccfu/ref/Bolt%26Weld.pdf). For a belt pull along the slot, let the jacking screw act as the backstop.

Use jack bolts rather than a hammer to shift a machine sideways, place them where they let you pivot the machine, and back them off once the hold-down bolts are tight (Ludeca, https://ludeca.com/blog/alignment/10070/using-jack-bolts-for-horizontal-correction-when-performing-shaft-alignment/).
Use the minimum belt tension that transmits the power without slipping; more shortens belt and bearing life (IronHorse instructions, as above).

everyday_examples: a 3D printer's X-axis motor that is slid along to tighten its belt (Prusa MK3/MK4)
a single-speed or track bike whose rear wheel slides in horizontal fork ends, pulled back by chain tugs (Sheldon Brown glossary)
a motorcycle's rear axle moved by two adjusting bolts to set chain slack (Honda owner's manual)
an older car's alternator, swung on a hinge and locked by a bolt in a curved slot to tension the fan belt (Wikimedia Commons photo)
guidance.when_to_use: When a belt or chain needs setting up once and re-tightening now and then as it stretches, and you can move one of the shafts (Gates prefers moving a shaft to adding an idler; the Belt tensioner entry agrees); when parts made with loose tolerances must be lined up on assembly; when you need more travel than an eccentric bush can give (the Eccentric adjuster entry suggests a slot when you need more than about twice the offset); for prototypes, where you don't yet know the exact centre distance. A jacking screw is worth adding whenever the part is heavy, the belt pull is strong, or you need fine, controlled moves.
guidance.when_not_to_use: When tension must stay right on its own as a belt stretches or the load changes: use a spring-loaded idler (Belt tensioner) or an automatic spring motor base (IronHorse). When a part must come back to exactly the same place every time: use locating pins or a hole-and-slot pair. For a very compact adjustment, an eccentric adjuster is neater. For setting tilt or height rather than sliding, use locking adjustment screws, shims or levelling feet. For continuous, powered movement use a lead screw. Avoid relying on friction alone along a slot under shock or vibration; add the jacking screw as a stop.
guidance.environment_limits: Vibration can loosen clamping and jacking screws; use lock nuts or thread-locker (general practice) [uncertain: no source opened for slotted mounts specifically]. Printed slotted brackets near warm motors creep and soften, PLA above about 60 °C (Prusa PLA page; Thrinter creep test). Outdoors, plain steel slides and screws rust and seize; galvanised or stainless parts last longer (industrial slide rails are galvanised steel, Soco). Rail tubes on automatic motor bases need greasing every 6 months (IronHorse instructions).
guidance.safety_notes: Belt and chain drives trap fingers, hair and clothing: switch off and unplug before adjusting, keep tools outside guards and refit guards afterwards (IronHorse instructions: 'Keep hands, tools, and clothing clear of any moving parts'). Over-tensioning overloads shafts and bearings (Gates; IronHorse). On road vehicles the axle adjusters also set wheel alignment; Honda says chain adjustment 'requires special tools' and to have it done by a dealer, so follow the vehicle's manual.
guidance.common_failures: (1) The part creeps back along the slot under belt pull and the belt goes slack: add or tighten the jacking screw as a backstop, use washers, and tighten the clamping screws properly (UMD/RCSC notes on slip along slots). (2) The part twists while the screws are tightened, misaligning the belt and wearing it on one edge: tighten evenly, move it with the adjusting screw only, turn twin adjusters by equal amounts and check marks (IronHorse; Honda; Gates on misalignment). (3) Not enough slot length left after the belt or chain stretches: design in the tensioning allowance (Gates; Tsubaki). (4) The printed thread for the jacking screw strips: use an insert or captive nut (Hubs; Printables 338646). (5) Screw heads sink into plastic or wood and the joint loosens: washers, harder material, re-tighten after settling (QIDI blog; Printables 217277). (6) Jack bolts left pressing after the hold-down bolts are tight, preloading the machine: back them off (Ludeca). (7) Over-tightened belts wear bearings (IronHorse).
related: Eccentric adjuster (eccentric nut, spacer or bushing): a compact turning adjustment with less travel
Belt tensioner (spring-loaded idler): keeps tension automatically instead of set-and-lock
Locking adjustment screws (push-pull screws, spring-loaded levelling screws): set tilt or height with opposing screws rather than sliding
Shims, spacers and standoffs: fixed packing to set a gap with no screw adjustment
Lead screw and nut: the same screw idea used to drive a part continuously
Turnbuckle: sets tension in a rod or cable by screwing
Locating pins and hole-and-slot: a slot used to locate a part exactly, not to adjust it
Aluminium-extrusion connectors (T-slot nuts and brackets): a continuous slot, so a mount can be slid anywhere along the extrusion and clamped
Dovetail slide with gib strip: a guided slide for parts that must move straight, with play taken up by a gib
Ordinary screw joint (bolt and nut): what it becomes once the screws are tightened
